opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about quite a bit, because a lot of my work has been on what we call the distributional simplicity bias: the idea that neural networks first pick up on the low-order statistics of their training data, like means and covariances, and only later start exploiting higher-order structure. Empirically, that pattern holds up surprisingly well across architectures and modalities.

Grokking looks, at first glance, like a counterexample. You train on something like modular arithmetic, the network quickly hits perfect training accuracy while test accuracy sits near chance, and then much later, sometimes orders of magnitude more steps later, it suddenly generalizes. So it seems to learn the "complex" thing first, a lookup table that memorizes every example, and only afterward finds the "simple" thing, the actual algorithm.

I think the resolution is that "simple" is doing a lot of work there, and there are different notions of simplicity that come apart. The memorizing solution isn't simple in a description-length sense; it's a huge lookup table. But it may be simple, or at least *easy*, from the perspective of gradient descent at initialization. It's reachable along a short path in parameter space, and it doesn't require coordinating many components into a structured circuit. The generalizing solution, say the Fourier-based algorithm people found for modular addition, is more compressible, but it requires a bunch of pieces to line up before it pays off in the loss.

Then weight decay, or whatever implicit regularization is in play, slowly pushes the network toward lower-norm solutions, and the generalizing circuit is lower-norm. So you get this slow phase where the generalizing circuit is quietly being built up while the memorization is being pruned away, and then the phase transition in test accuracy is just the point where the cleanup finishes.

The other thing worth saying is that the tasks where grokking shows up most dramatically are kind of adversarial to a distributional simplicity bias. In modular arithmetic with uniformly sampled inputs, the low-order statistics carry essentially no information about the label. There's no cheap linear or quadratic shortcut to grab first. So the network can't do its usual thing of learning the easy statistical approximation and refining from there. It has to either memorize or find the full algorithm. In that sense grokking is less a refutation of simplicity bias and more what happens when you remove the simple stepping stones the network normally relies on.

So I'd frame it as an exception that's informative about the boundary conditions. Simplicity bias describes the typical trajectory when the data has graded structure, and grokking shows what learning looks like when that graded structure isn't there.

r001.rationale: The response describes grokking as taking orders of magnitude more steps, but does not mention a logarithmic training-time axis making it appear faster.

r002.rationale: It says weight decay or implicit regularization pushes toward lower-norm solutions and favors the lower-norm generalizing circuit over memorization.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, because on its face grokking looks like a counterexample to the simplicity bias story. The story is that networks pick up low-order, simple structure first and then gradually layer on more complex structure. And grokking looks like the opposite: the network memorizes the training set, which seems like the "complex" thing, and then only much later does it find the clean, generalizing algorithm, which seems like the "simple" thing.

But I actually don't think it's a real exception. I think it's an artifact of conflating two different notions of simplicity.

When we say networks learn simple functions first, the sense of simplicity that's actually operative in the dynamics is something like low sensitivity, or low frequency in the Fourier sense, or low degree if you think in terms of polynomial expansions. It's a statistical, input-output notion of complexity. It's not Kolmogorov complexity. It's not "how short is the program that describes this."

The modular arithmetic task that grokking was first observed on is kind of adversarial with respect to that statistical notion. The target function is maximally high frequency. Flip one bit of the input, or change one operand by one, and the output changes essentially randomly from the perspective of any low-order statistic. There are no low-degree features to grab onto. So the simplicity bias has nothing to work with early in training, and what happens instead is the network just uses its capacity to fit the training points. Memorization in that regime is actually the lowest-sensitivity thing available that gets the loss down, because it only commits to behavior on the points it's seen.

Then with weight decay and a lot of time, the optimizer finds the trig or Fourier circuit solution, which has a very short description but is extremely high frequency as a function. And at that point the network has no reason to keep the memorization machinery around, so it decays away and you see the sharp jump in test accuracy.

So from the Kolmogorov point of view it looks like complex then simple. From the sensitivity or degree point of view, it's low sensitivity then high sensitivity, which is exactly what the simplicity bias predicts. The order is preserved. It's just that the task was constructed so that the generalizing solution is on the hard side of the gradient rather than the easy side.

And I think the evidence supports this reading. If you look at the training dynamics in more natural settings, the low-degree stuff really does come first. Grokking shows up primarily on these algorithmic tasks with small training sets and strong regularization, where the only correct hypothesis is one the bias actively disfavors. The delay is the cost of swimming upstream. That's not the bias failing; that's the bias doing what it does on a task where the right answer happens to be unsimple in the relevant sense.

So I'd put it this way: grokking isn't an exception to simplicity first. It's a demonstration that the kind of simplicity networks care about isn't the kind humans naturally reach for when they look at the closed-form solution and say "but that's so elegant."

r001.rationale: The response does not mention a logarithmic training-time axis or say that it makes grokking appear faster.

r002.rationale: It says weight decay accompanies the late discovery of the Fourier circuit, but does not attribute the shift to regularization favoring simpler models. It instead emphasizes that the circuit is high-frequency and simple only in the Kolmogorov-description sense.

astra-6.text:
I think grokking is a useful qualification to that idea. In the classic setup, the network first memorizes the training set. Training accuracy becomes very high, but generalization stays poor. Then, if you keep training, sometimes for much longer, it starts generalizing.

If you think of simplicity in terms of description length, the generalizing solution can be much simpler than the memorizing solution. A compact rule for modular arithmetic is simpler than a lookup table of all the training examples. So in that sense, the more complex function comes first, and the simpler function comes later.

But the important distinction is between a function being simple and a function being easy for gradient descent to find. Memorization can be accessible through local improvements to the loss, whereas discovering a shared algorithm can require representations to develop together. And regularization, like weight decay, can eventually favor that more compact solution.

So I wouldn’t say grokking shows that networks have no simplicity bias. It shows that a simplicity bias isn’t necessarily an ordering principle where every stage of training gives you a more complex function than the previous stage.

r001.rationale: The response says grokking may take much longer, but does not mention a logarithmic training-time axis making it appear faster.

r002.rationale: It says regularization such as weight decay can eventually favor the more compact, simpler solution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think grokking complicates what we mean by “simple.” In the classic setup, you train a network on something like modular arithmetic, and it first memorizes the training examples. Training accuracy gets very high, but test accuracy stays low. Then, after much more training, it suddenly starts generalizing.

One way to understand that is that the memorizing solution is easier to find, even though the generalizing solution has a simpler underlying structure. So simplicity in the sense of a short algorithm isn’t necessarily the same as simplicity from the optimizer’s perspective.

With something like weight decay, you can gradually favor that more compact solution over the memorizing one. And the sudden jump in test accuracy doesn’t necessarily mean the underlying learning happened suddenly; there can be a gradual change that only becomes visible in accuracy once you cross a threshold. So I’d take grokking as a warning against treating “simple functions are learned first” as a universal rule.

r001.rationale: The response describes a delayed, sudden-looking jump in test accuracy, but does not mention a logarithmic training-time axis making grokking appear faster.

r002.rationale: It says weight decay can favor the more compact solution over the memorizing one, attributing the shift to regularization favoring simpler models.
